    {
      "startEvent": 711,
      "endEvent": 722,
      "contextStartEvent": 654,
      "contextEndEvent": 788,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "I think the physical resurrection is totally unimportant",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "none"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Ruse excludes physical verification from what matters religiously, locating significance in the disciples’ changed outlook (E714–722). This could protect that interpretation from historical objections, but he distinguishes spiritual meaning from a literal claim rather than proving the latter regardless of evidence. His later refusal to argue (E766–775) leaves the protective scope uncertain."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1192,
      "endEvent": 1204,
      "contextStartEvent": 1151,
      "contextEndEvent": 1284,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "I think that God is a God who knows how to compensate",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": [
        "comfort"
      ],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Future judgment and compensation answer the Himmler–Anne Frank objection without explaining how compensation justifies permitting those harms (E1192–1204). Unspecified future redress could insulate divine goodness, but Lennox says only that questions might become less severe. He acknowledges terrible problems and adds a freedom-and-love argument at E1256–1284, preventing a clear every-outcome-confirms finding."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1130,
      "endEvent": 1150,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "but I think they're open to theological and philosophical criticism",
      "explanation": "Ruse explains why a mechanical description leaves certain questions unanswered, permits Christian answers, and explicitly subjects them to criticism. The distinction is developed through examples rather than asserted as a closing slogan."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1064,
      "endEvent": 1099,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "I can't solve it I wouldn't pretend to",
      "explanation": "Lennox presents the cross and resurrection conditionally as grounds for hope, acknowledges the world's mixed evidence, and distinguishes trust from solving the problem of suffering. His cathedral metaphor summarizes that qualified account."
    }
  ]
